new_statements.translation: 2.1.4. Stress. Primary stress falls regularly on the last syllable of words. /ama/ 'mother'. Secondary stress commonly occurs on alternate syllables counting backwards from the primary-stressed syllable in verbs without suffixes. When a noun is affixed, the primary stress may move to the last syllable of the new word or stay on the final syllable of the root. It will frequently fall in the place of the secondary stress. /ka'i-a pere/ 'the monkey's liver' ... If the noun occurs at the end of a sentence, the suffix takes the stress. /yenepomomap hãy-a/ 'five teeth'.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very source of the catalog's fixed-strict record (final primary, alternating secondaries leftward: alternating stress from the right); the catalog_quote is §2.1.4 of this work verbatim. The only nuance beyond the strict grid is the optional root-final primary in suffixed nouns, which the catalog quote already carries.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable: primary stress on the word-final syllable; secondary stresses on alternate syllables leftward from the primary (stated for unsuffixed verbs in §2.1.4 and as the general regularity 'a contar da última sílaba das palavras' in §4.3). With suffixed nouns the primary stress either moves to the new final syllable or stays on the root-final syllable (then landing where a secondary would be); sentence-finally the suffix carries the stress. Stress placement is used as a non-contrastive diagnostic in §4.2 ('Não há na língua Kamayurá evidência para tal contraste').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating, right-to-left from the primary: §2.1.4 p.134 'O acento secundário ocorre comumente em silabas alternativas a contar para trás da sílaba de acentuação primária em verbos sem sufixos'; §4.3 p.143 '[i].. É necessário que seja considerado vogal para que a acentuação secundária seja regular, caindo nas silabas alternativas a contar da Última silaba das palavras. /nikaramemaite/ [níkarámemáite] 'Ele não tem coisas''.
new_statements.exceptions: Affixed nouns: primary stress may shift to the final syllable of the affixed word or remain on the root-final syllable (variation); a sentence-final noun's suffix takes the stress. Loanwords from Portuguese and other regional languages are excluded from the study (§1). Emphatic intonation lengthens the stressed syllable (§2.1.8.2); onset stops of stressed syllables lengthen (§2.1.7).
new_statements.identity_note: Kamayurá (Tupi-Guarani, Upper Xingu, Parque Nacional do Xingu), data from the Kamayurá village collected Oct 1973 - Aug 1974 by Meinke Saelzer (SIL); loanwords excluded.

sources.note: A comparative metrical STRESS thesis, secondhand for Kamaiurá (data from Salzer 1976 and Seki 2000): stress is root-final, non-contrastive, iambic right-to-left with alternating secondary stress, and its phonetic correlates are pitch (altura) and intensity; no lexical tone is posited or discussed for Kamaiurá (tone appears only in the general theory chapter). Not a tone work - listed because it is a new open prosody source bearing on tonality (pitch = stress correlate) and on the stress record.

tone.quote: Seki (2000), por sua vez, afirma que o acento recai sempre na última sílaba do radical (formas livres), não é contrastivo e tem como correlatos fonéticos altura e intensidade.
tone.locator: p.72, sec. 5.3.1 'O que os estudiosos dizem sobre o acento em Kamaiurá'
tone.translation: Seki (2000), in turn, states that stress always falls on the last syllable of the root (free forms), is not contrastive, and has pitch and intensity as its phonetic correlates.
tone.summary: Non-tonal: pitch reported only as a correlate of predictable final stress (after Seki 2000:419).
